Score: 1 for Industrial Hemp--0 for DEA

by Rep. Cynthia Thielen, Hawaii
February 26, 1998

The County Council of Kauai (the elected governing body for the Island of Kauai) held two comprehensive hearings on the "marijuana" Resolution. Several proponents of industrial hemp research appeared, including myself, and faced off with the DEA. The DEA opposed any language supporting industrial hemp.

The Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) asked the County Councils to pass a Resolution asking us in the Legislature not to pass any laws relating to "marijuana." DEA worded the Resolution so broadly that it could have impacted upon our legislative efforts to permit industrial hemp test plots to be planted.

by Rep. Cynthia Thielen, Hawaii
February 26, 1998

The County Council of Kauai (the elected governing body for the Island of Kauai) held two comprehensive hearings on the "marijuana" Resolution. Several proponents of industrial hemp research appeared, including myself, and faced off with the DEA. The DEA opposed any language supporting industrial hemp.

The Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) asked the County Councils to pass a Resolution asking us in the Legislature not to pass any laws relating to "marijuana." DEA worded the Resolution so broadly that it could have impacted upon our legislative efforts to permit industrial hemp test plots to be planted.

The County Council of Kauai (the elected governing body for the Island of Kauai) held two comprehensive hearings on the "marijuana" Resolution. Several proponents of industrial hemp research appeared, including myself, and faced off with the DEA. The DEA opposed any language supporting industrial hemp.

At the end of the second hearing on February 18, the entire County Council Committee (comprised of all council members) passed out a strongly worded Resolution in favor of industrial hemp research plots. They clearly recognized the economic potential of this crop for Kauai’s ag land.

I believe this is a major break-through. An elected body, where each member runs for reelection this year, had the courage to say No to the DEA and instead vote in support of this agronomic research.

The hearings were televised on Kauai and rerun a number of times, and the local print media covered the event very well. Of all locales in Hawaii, I would say that Island is very well educated about industrial hemp and supportive of our efforts.

In contrast, the Chair of the House Agricultural Committee lacked the courage to even hear the industrial hemp bill. But this won’t stop the research test plots! DEA publicly stated before the Kauai County Council and in quotes to the media that state law does not need to be changed in order for these test plots to proceed. DEA claims the ag corporations only need to get a DEA permit and State Narcotics Division permit to be authorized to conduct the research.

We have informed the Chief of Staff of US Senator Dan Inouye of the DEA’s statements along with the fact that we now have two major companies in Hawaii and one farmer that want to go ahead with the research. The Director of Business and Economic Development is writing DEA in Washington, DC to obtain more permit applications. We will keep Senator Inouye’s staff apprised of the status and will ask his help in making sure DEA processes the permit applications in a timely manner and without placing undue restrictions on the corporations. Given the economic crisis in Hawaii and the large number of vacant agricultural acres, I do not believe the Senator will accept stonewalling by DEA.

This experience has taught me that we should use as many avenues as we can think up to get the hemp test plots moving. I suggest you talk with ag companies, educate them about the issue, work with your State business development sections, and keep your US Congresspeople informed and ready to help. If the requests for permit applications come from across the nation, coupled with support from state business officials, and if ag companies step up to be a part of this effort, and Congresspeople become involved to at least "monitor the status", then I believe we’ll begin to break down the barriers.

Let’s keep building on each others success, and on the information we’ll be gaining from Canada. At this point, I’ve told colleagues in the House of Representatives that we’re going ahead—forget the bill, and march right by the cowardly Chair. Somehow, I’m reminded of the Wizzard of OZ—who was it that asked the Wizzard for courage? And remeber, Dorothy made it back to the farm where, I’ll bet, industrial hemp was growing in the fields!

Representative Cynthia Thielen

Hawaii State Capitol

Honolulu, HI 96813
